full_text_en:
Warner-Lambert Company LLC v. Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China et al. — administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent

【Ruling Summary】

I. In a patent specification for a product invention in the chemical field, the identification, preparation, and use of the chemical product shall be recorded.

II. There is a logical sequential relationship between the reproducibility of the technical solution of a product invention in the chemical field and the evaluation of whether the technical problem is solved and technical effects are produced. It shall first be determined whether a person of ordinary skill in the art can realize the technical solution based on the contents disclosed in the specification, and then whether the technical problem is solved and technical effects are produced.

III. Experimental evidence submitted after the filing date for the purpose of proving sufficient disclosure in the specification, if it can prove that a person of ordinary skill in the art, based on the knowledge level and cognitive ability before the filing date, can realize the invention through the contents disclosed in the specification, shall be considered and cannot be rejected merely because it was submitted after the filing date.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Judgment

(2014) Xing Ti Zi No. 8

Re-applicant (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China. Domicile: 10-12/F, Yingu Building, No. 9, North Fourth Ring West Road, Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Agent ad litem: Huang Zexiong, male, Han Chinese, born February 7, 1957, patent agent of Beijing Bangxinyang Patent & Trademark Agency Co., Ltd., residing at 14/F, Building 10, Madian Guancheng Nanyuan, Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Warner-Lambert Company LLC. Domicile: 235 E. 42nd ST, New York, NY 10017, U.S.A.

Legal Representative: J. Michael Dixon, Legal Counsel of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Long Chuanhong, male, Han Chinese, born May 2, 1969, patent agent of China Council for the Promotion of International Trade Patent and Trademark Office, residing in Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.

The re-applicants, the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board) and Beijing Jialin Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Jialin Company), dissatisfied with the administrative judgment (2010) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 1489 rendered by the Beijing High People's Court in the case concerning the administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent rights with the respondent Warner-Lambert Company LLC and the third party at first instance Zhang Chu, filed a request for retrial with this Court. This Court issued an administrative ruling (2013) Zhi Xing Zi No. 16 on December 11, 2013, to retry the case. This Lawful formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing on October 20, 2014. The agents ad litem of the Patent Reexamination Board Wang Xiaodong and Pan Jun, the agents ad litem of Jialin Company Huang Zexiong and Fan Yaofeng, the agents ad litem of Warner-Lambert Company Long Chuanhong and Lin Sen, and the agent ad litem of Zhang Chu Miao Renkang appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The case is now concluded.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court found at first instance:

On July 8, 1996, Warner-Lambert Company filed an invention patent application entitled "Crystalline [R-(R*,R*)]-2-(4-fluorophenyl)-beta,delta-dihydroxy-5-(1-methylethyl)-3-phenyl-4-[(phenylamino)carbonyl]-1H-pyrrole-1-heptanoic acid hemicalcium salt" (i.e., the patent in question), which was granted on July 10, 2002, with patent number 96195564.3. The priority date of the patent in question is July 17, 1995.

The claims of the patent in question are:

A method for preparing Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water, the method comprising: step (a) suspending a mixture of amorphous atorvastatin and Type I crystalline atorvastatin in water containing a cosolvent; and step (b) isolating the Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate.

Page 15 of the specification of the patent in question states: "The Type I, Type II, and Type IV crystalline atorvastatin of the present invention may exist in anhydrous forms as well as hydrated forms. In general, the hydrated forms are equivalent to the non-hydrated forms and are included within the scope of the present invention. Type I crystalline atorvastatin contains about 1 to 8 moles of water. Preferably, Type I crystalline atorvastatin contains 3 moles of water." "The present invention provides a method for preparing Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate, the method comprising: step (a), treating an aqueous solution of an alkaline salt of crystalline [R-(R*,R*)]-2-(4-fluorophenyl)-beta,delta-dihydroxy-5-(1-methylethyl)-3-phenyl-4-[(phenylamino)carbonyl]-1H-pyrrole-1-heptanoic acid with a calcium salt; step (b), isolating Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate."

Page 17 of the specification of the patent in question states: "For example, when the starting material is Type I crystalline atorvastatin, the desired Type IV crystalline atorvastatin can be prepared by dissolving the solid in methanol and then precipitating Type IV crystals."

Pages 19 to 20 of the specification of the patent in question state: "Example 1, [R-(R*,R*)]-2-(4-fluorophenyl)-beta,delta-dihydroxy-5-(1-methylethyl)-3-phenyl-4-[(phenylamino)carbonyl]-1H-pyrrole-1-heptanoic acid hemicalcium salt (Type I atorvastatin). Method A: At 48-58°C, a mixture of (2R-trans)-5-(4-fluorophenyl)-2-(1-methylethyl)-N,4-diphenyl-1-[2-(tetrahydro-4-hydroxy-6-oxo-2H-pyran-2-yl)ethyl]-1H-pyrrole-3-carboxamide (atorvastatin lactone) (US5273995) (75 kg), methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE) (308 kg), and methanol (190 L) is reacted with an aqueous sodium hydroxide solution (5.72 kg NaOH in 950 L water) for 40-60 minutes to form the ring-opened sodium salt. After cooling to 25-35°C, the organic layer is discarded, and the aqueous layer is extracted again with MTBE (230 kg). The organic layer is discarded, and the MTBE-saturated aqueous sodium salt solution is heated to 47-52°C. A solution of calcium acetate hemihydrate (11.94 kg) dissolved in water (410 L) is added to this solution over at least 30 minutes. Shortly after the addition of the calcium acetate solution, the mixture is seeded with a slurry of Type I crystalline atorvastatin (1.1 kg atorvastatin in 11 L water and 5 L methanol). The mixture is then heated to 51-57°C for at least 10 minutes, then cooled to 15-40°C. The mixture is filtered, and the filter cake is washed with a solution of water (300 L) and methanol (150 L), then with water (450 L). The solid is dried under vacuum at 60-70°C for 3-4 days to obtain Type I crystalline atorvastatin (72.2 kg). Method B: Amorphous atorvastatin (9 g) and Type I crystalline atorvastatin (1 g) are stirred at about 40°C in a mixture of water (170 mL) and methanol (30 mL) for 17 hours. The mixture is filtered, washed with water, and dried at 70°C under reduced pressure to obtain Type I crystalline atorvastatin (9.7 g)."

Pages 20 to 21 of the specification of the patent in question state: "Example 3, [R-(R*,R*)]-2-(4-fluorophenyl)-beta,delta-dihydroxy-5-(1-methylethyl)-3-phenyl-4-[(phenylamino)carbonyl]-1H-pyrrole-1-heptanoic acid hemicalcium salt (Type IV atorvastatin). At 50-55°C, a mixture of (2R-trans)-5-(4-fluorophenyl)-2-(1-methylethyl)-N,4-diphenyl-1-[2-(tetrahydro-4-hydroxy-6-oxo-2H-pyran-2-yl)ethyl]-1H-pyrrole-3-carboxamide (atorvastatin lactone) (US5273995) (12 kg), MTBE (50 kg), and methanol (30 L) is reacted with an aqueous sodium hydroxide solution (1.83 kg NaOH in 150 L water) for 30-45 minutes to form the ring-opened sodium salt. After cooling to 20-25°C, the organic layer is discarded, and the aqueous layer is extracted again with MTBE (37 kg). The aqueous layer is discarded, and the aqueous sodium salt solution is heated to 70-80°C, and residual MTBE is removed by distillation. The solution is then cooled to 60-70°C. A solution of calcium acetate hemihydrate (1.91 kg) dissolved in water/methanol (72 L water + 16 L methanol) is added to this solution. Shortly after the addition of the calcium acetate solution, the mixture is seeded with Type I crystalline atorvastatin (180 g). The mixture is heated to 65-75°C for at least 5 minutes, then cooled to 50-55°C. The mixture is filtered, and the filter cake is slurried in methanol (about 200 L) at 55-65°C, then cooled to 25-30°C and filtered. The solid is dried under vacuum at 66-70°C to obtain Type IV crystalline atorvastatin (about 3 kg isolated)."

Jialin Company, as one of the requestors for invalidation, filed a request for invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board regarding the validity of the patent in question, including the following grounds: 1. The claims of the patent in question protect Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water, which includes eight types of Type I crystals, but the specification does not verify that these eight types of Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate have the same XPRD and 13CNMR data; 2. Based on either the general disclosure in the specification or the disclosure of the examples, a person of ordinary skill in the art would have difficulty preparing Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water.

On June 17, 2009, the Patent Reexamination Board issued Examination Decision No. 13582 on the Request for Invalidation (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 13582) in response to Jialin Company's request for invalidation of the patent in question. The decision made the following findings: Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law) provides that the specification shall clearly and completely describe the invention so that a person of ordinary skill in the art can realize it. For a chemical product invention, "a person of ordinary skill in the art can realize" means that a person of ordinary skill in the art can identify and prepare the chemical product based on the contents disclosed in the specification, and can realize one or more of its uses and/or achieve the corresponding use effects. Specifically, when the chemical product is a compound crystal, on the one hand, the specification shall not only describe the material composition and crystal structure of the compound crystal, but also record the corresponding physicochemical parameters (such as qualitative or quantitative data and spectra) that can prove the material composition and microstructure of the crystal; on the other hand, the specification shall also record at least one preparation method for the compound crystal so that a person of ordinary skill in the art can implement it. Conversely, if a person of ordinary skill in the art cannot confirm the material composition or microstructure of the compound crystal based on the preparation method disclosed in the specification, or cannot be convinced whether the compound crystal can be obtained based on the preparation method disclosed in the specification, then the disclosure of the compound crystal in the specification has not reached the level that a person of ordinary skill in the art can realize.

In this case, Claims 1-3 seek to protect a Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water, which is defined by two characterization methods: first, the composition, i.e., atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 (or 3) moles of water; second, the XPRD and 13CNMR data characterizing its microstructure. Jialin Company argued that the specification did not sufficiently disclose the Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as claimed in the patent in question. The reasons are: the claim protects Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water, which includes eight types of Type I crystals, but the specification does not verify that these eight types of crystalline hydrates have the same XPRD and 13CNMR data; regardless of whether it is based on the general disclosure in the specification or the disclosure of the examples, a person of ordinary skill in the art would have difficulty preparing Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water. In response, Warner-Lambert Company argued that the specification disclosed the structure and its analytical data of the Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as claimed in the patent in question, as well as its preparation method, preparation examples, and beneficial effects. Counter-evidence 9, a 1982 publication, proves that water in hydrate crystals can exist as water of crystallization or not as water of crystallization. The present patent falls under the latter, and therefore, the patent in question complies with the provisions of Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

The main points of dispute between the parties are: first, whether the XRPD and 13C NMR spectra of hydrates of the same compound containing different molar amounts of water are identical; and second, whether the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as claimed in the patent can be confirmed and prepared based on the content disclosed in the patent specification.

Regarding the first point of dispute, Jialin argued that crystalline hydrates containing different amounts of water of crystallization must necessarily have different XRPD patterns, while Warner-Lambert relied on Counterevidence 9 to contend that in hydrates, water may exist as water of crystallization or may not exist in that form. The Patent Reexamination Board found that the Chinese translation of Counterevidence 9, lines 1-3, disclosed the following: "Unlike the behavior of caffeine, theophylline, and mercaptopurine, the X-ray powder diffraction patterns of solvated and non-solvated crystalline forms of cefalexin (15) and cephalexin (16) are almost identical (Pfeiffer et al., 1970)." That is, Counterevidence 9 confirmed that for cefalexin and cephalexin, solvated and non-solvated crystals have almost identical XRPD patterns, but this is not the case for caffeine, theophylline, and mercaptopurine. Thus, on the one hand, in this field, not all water in hydrates of substances occupies positions in the unit cell to generate different XRPD patterns; on the other hand, for a given substance, whether the water in its hydrate will occupy positions, and whether the presence or amount of water will affect its XRPD pattern, is not uniformly taught in the art.

Regarding the second point of dispute, the Patent Reexamination Board found that for the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water protected by the patent-in-suit, the specification disclosed the following relevant content: the last paragraph on page 2 to line 8 on page 4, Table 1 on page 9, and Table 4 on page 12 disclosed XRPD and 13C NMR data for the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate. Lines 15-19 on page 15 of the specification stated: "The I-type crystalline atorvastatin of this patent may exist in anhydrous forms as well as hydrated forms. Generally, the hydrated forms are equivalent to the non-hydrated forms and are included within the scope of this patent. I-type crystalline atorvastatin contains about 1 to 8 moles of water, preferably 3 moles of water." Lines 20 on page 15 to page 16 gave a general method for preparing the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate. Method A of Example 1 on pages 19-20 described a method for preparing I-type crystals using an aqueous solution of the sodium salt as a starting material, treated with an aqueous solution of calcium acetate and a seed crystal of I-type crystals. Method B described a method for preparing I-type crystals using a mixture of an amorphous solution and I-type crystalline atorvastatin as a starting material. From the above, it can be seen that: 1. Warner-Lambert's assertion regarding the equivalency of hydrated and non-hydrated forms of atorvastatin was limited to its own statement. That is, it claimed that the presence of water does not affect the XRPD of the crystals, but provided no evidence to prove this. Based on the findings above, for a given substance, whether the water in its hydrate will occupy positions, and whether the presence or amount of water will affect its XRPD, is not uniformly taught in the art. A person skilled in the art, based on common general knowledge, could not predict whether atorvastatin belongs to the category of substances in which water does not occupy positions and does not affect XRPD, or to the category in which water does occupy positions and affects XRPD. Under these circumstances, the specification should provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate whether for atorvastatin hydrates containing different molar amounts of water, they have the same XRPD pattern. Where the specification only contains a conclusory statement without corresponding evidence, a person skilled in the art cannot be convinced that atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water have the same XRPD pattern. 2. The crystalline products protected by claims 1-3 are defined by both their composition (atorvastatin, water content) and their microstructure (XRPD and 13C NMR). Water content is an essential part of the product composition. However, the specification only stated that the water content is 1-8 moles, preferably 3 moles, but provided no qualitative or quantitative data to prove that the obtained I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate indeed contained 1-8 moles (preferably 3 moles) of water. Even the most specific Example 1 did not measure the water content of the product. Moreover, based on the steps of the preparation method and the XRPD and 13C NMR data and spectra used to characterize the crystal form of the product, it could not be definitively inferred that the product necessarily contained water, let alone that the water content was 1-8 moles (or 3 moles). Therefore, a person skilled in the art could not, based on the content disclosed in the specification, confirm the product protected by the claims. 3. Regarding the preparation of atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water, the specification disclosed a general preparation method, namely, comprising step (a): treating an aqueous solution of an alkali metal salt of crystalline [R-(R*,R*)]-2-(4-fluorophenyl)-β,δ-dihydroxy-5-(1-methylethyl)-3-phenyl-4-[(phenylamino)carbonyl]-1H-pyrrole-1-heptanoic acid with a calcium salt; and step (b): isolating the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate. However, comparing Method A of Example 1 of the patent-in-suit with Example 3, both contain steps (a) and (b), but the former yields I-type crystals containing 1-8 moles of water, while the latter yields IV-type crystals. Therefore, the general method alone cannot definitively yield atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water. The specification on page 16 refined the general method, and Method A of Example 1 provided a specific scheme. However, since Example 1 only stated that it obtained I-type crystalline atorvastatin without measuring the water content of the product, one could not be convinced from Example 1 that the method would necessarily yield atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water. Therefore, a person skilled in the art, whether based on the general method given in the specification or on the specific example, could not be convinced how to controllably prepare the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water (preferably 3 moles) as protected by the patent-in-suit.

In summary, the Patent Reexamination Board held that the disclosure of the crystalline products protected by claims 1-3 in the specification did not reach the level enabling implementation by a person skilled in the art, and therefore did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law. On this basis, claims 4-9, which protect pharmaceutical compositions comprising the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as defined in claims 1-3, and claims 10-24, which protect methods for preparing the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as defined in claims 1-3, also did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

Warner-Lambert argued that the example is generally a preferred embodiment, so the product obtained in Method A of Example 1 should have a water content of 3 moles. In response, the Patent Reexamination Board held that this was still an assertion made by Warner-Lambert without supporting evidence.

In light of the above, the Patent Reexamination Board declared the patent-in-suit invalid in its entirety.

Warner-Lambert, dissatisfied with this decision, filed a lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, requesting the revocation of Decision No. 13582 made by the Patent Reexamination Board.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held that the disputed issues in this case were:

1. Whether the XRPD patterns of I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrates containing different molar amounts of water as claimed in the patent-in-suit are identical.

Warner-Lambert acknowledged that for a given substance, whether the water in its hydrate will occupy positions, and whether the presence or amount of water will affect its XRPD, is not uniformly taught in the art. Warner-Lambert argued that page 15 of the specification of the patent-in-suit stated that the I-type, II-type, and IV-type crystalline atorvastatin of the patent may exist in anhydrous forms as well as hydrated forms, and that generally, the hydrated forms are equivalent to the non-hydrated forms. This statement indicated that the water of crystallization in this patent would not affect the XRPD of the crystals. The Patent Reexamination Board held that this statement in the specification was merely a claim, lacking evidence to prove the conclusion, and therefore a person skilled in the art could not be convinced that atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water have the same XRPD pattern. Jialin argued that the statement "Generally, the hydrated forms are equivalent to the non-hydrated forms" in the specification lacked supporting evidence. Jialin and Zhang Chu both agreed with the Patent Reexamination Board.

2. Whether, based on the content disclosed in the specification of the patent-in-suit, it can be confirmed that the obtained I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate contains 1-8 moles of water.

Warner-Lambert acknowledged that the specification did not measure how much water the obtained I-type crystalline atorvastatin contained, and also acknowledged that the water content of the corresponding compound could not be determined from the spectra disclosed in the specification alone. However, Warner-Lambert argued that confirming the molar amount of water in the product was easy, because methods for determining the water content of compounds were common general knowledge in the art, such as the Karl Fischer titration method. The Patent Reexamination Board held that even if the method for determining water content was itself publicly known, since the sample to be measured was uncertain, the common general knowledge argument was irrelevant to this case. Jialin argued that the Karl Fischer titration method can only measure total water content, not the amount of water of crystallization in the hydrate, and therefore the water content of the I-type crystalline atorvastatin obtained in Example 1 could not be determined by this method.

3. Whether, based on the content disclosed in the specification of the patent-in-suit, the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water could be prepared.

Warner-Lambert argued that the specification of the patent-in-suit disclosed one example for preparing the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate of the patent, namely, Method A of Example 1. Although Method A of Example 1 did not explicitly state that the obtained product contained 3 moles of water, page 15 of the specification stated that "I-type crystalline atorvastatin contains about 1 to 8 moles of water. Preferably, I-type crystalline atorvastatin contains 3 moles of water." That is, the preferred embodiment was I-type crystalline atorvastatin containing 3 moles of water. When the patent-in-suit was filed in 1996, the applicable version was the 1993 Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Implementing Regulations"). Article 18, Paragraph 1, Item 8 of those Regulations provided: "Describe in detail the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention or utility model, and where appropriate, illustrate by way of examples; if there are drawings, refer to them." The phrase "illustrate by way of examples" is a mandatory provision. From this, it can be inferred that Method A of Example 1 in the specification of the patent-in-suit corresponds to the preferred embodiment of containing 3 moles of water described on page 15 of the specification. That is, whether water is present and how many molecules of water are present have been substantively disclosed. The Patent Reexamination Board disagreed. First, the applicable version of the Implementing Regulations in this case is the 2001 version. Second, the phrase "illustrate by way of examples" is not a mandatory provision but a recommendatory one, because even if the specification is not written in accordance with this provision, the patent will not be rejected or declared invalid on that ground. Therefore, there is no logic that Example 1 necessarily corresponds to the preferred embodiment, nor can it be determined that the product obtained in Method A of Example 1 of the patent-in-suit is the product containing 3 moles of water referred to in the preferred embodiment.

Warner-Lambert further argued that page 17 of the specification clearly stated: "When the starting material is I-type crystalline atorvastatin, the desired IV-type crystalline atorvastatin can be prepared by dissolving the solid in methanol and then allowing the IV-type crystals to precipitate." In Example 3 of the specification, I-type crystalline atorvastatin was first obtained by a method identical to that of Example 1, then subjected to crystal form conversion with methanol, and finally IV-type crystals were obtained. Therefore, the finding in Decision No. 13582 that "a person skilled in the art, whether based on the general method given in the specification or on the specific example, could not be convinced how to controllably prepare the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water (preferably 3 moles) as protected by the patent-in-suit" was unfounded. The Patent Reexamination Board adhered to the opinion expressed in the last paragraph on page 25 through the first paragraph on page 26 of Decision No. 13582.

The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held in the first instance that claims 1-3 of the patent-in-suit protect an I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water, which is defined by both the water composition and the microstructure. First, regarding the microstructure of the hydrate, whether I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water have the same XRPD pattern, since the prior art provides no uniform teaching, and the specification contains only a conclusory statement "Generally, the hydrated forms are equivalent to the non-hydrated forms" without experimental verification, based on the current evidence, it cannot be considered that I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water have the same XRPD pattern. Second, based on the description in the specification, whether the I-type crystalline atorvastatin contains water is uncertain. The "total water content" measured by the "Karl Fischer water determination method" may include the sum of both possible water of crystallization and/or various forms of non-crystalline water, and it cannot be determined that it is the relatively stable water of crystallization combined with the compound molecule. Whether the I-type crystalline atorvastatin contains 1-8 moles of water remains unknown. At the same time, with respect to the confirmation of the compound, the specification did not confirm one of the components of the obtained chemical product, namely the water content. Regardless of whether the method for determining the water content of the compound was publicly known before the filing date, this cannot change the fact that the specification should have disclosed but failed to disclose such content. Finally, regarding the preparation of the compound, examination can be conducted from two aspects: the specific example and the general method. First, regarding Method A of Example 1, which is the only specific preparation method corresponding to claims 1-3, the method did not measure the water content of its product, so it cannot be confirmed that implementing this method can prepare the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water. At the same time, whether under the 1993 or the 2001 version of the Implementing Regulations, Article 18 is a recommendatory provision, not a mandatory one. Even if the specification is not written in accordance with this provision, the patent will not be rejected or declared invalid on that ground. This provision is not a legal basis for determining whether a patent should be rejected or declared invalid. Warner-Lambert's argument that setting a preferred embodiment must correspond to Method A of Example 1, and thus deriving that the technical solution containing 3 moles of water has been disclosed, cannot be established. The reasons are as follows: 1. This argument and inference lack factual and legal basis and are not persuasive. 2. This argument and inference violate common logic. Based on the description in the specification, whether the I-type crystalline atorvastatin obtained by Method A of Example 1 contains water and how many moles of water it contains are uncertain issues, and from this, it cannot be uniquely derived that what is obtained by Method A of Example 1 is the preferred I-type crystalline atorvastatin containing 3 moles of water. 3. This argument was proposed by Warner-Lambert and is advantageous to Warner-Lambert, so it is reasonable that Warner-Lambert bears the burden of proof. Warner-Lambert's assertion that the Patent Reexamination Board should bear the burden of proving that the product does not contain 3 moles of water violates the rules of evidence. Second, Warner-Lambert's claim that "in Example 3, IV-type crystalline atorvastatin was first obtained by a method identical to Method A of Example 1 to obtain I-type crystals, and then this I-type crystal was subjected to crystal form conversion in methanol to obtain IV-type crystals" lacks factual basis.

In summary, the specification of the patent-in-suit neither confirmed the water content of the obtained compound nor experimentally verified that I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water have the same XRPD pattern. Therefore, the disclosure of the crystalline products protected by claims 1-3 in the specification did not reach the level enabling implementation by a person skilled in the art, and did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law. On this basis, claims 4-9, which protect pharmaceutical compositions comprising the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as defined in claims 1-3, and claims 10-24, which protect methods for preparing the I-type crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as defined in claims 1-3, also did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law. Pursuant to Article 54, Paragraph (1) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court rendered judgment: Decision No. 13582 was upheld.

Warner-Lambert Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court, arguing as follows: (1) The experimental report titled "Preparation and Identification Experiment Report of Atorvastatin Calcium Crystals" completed by Associate Professor Gong Junbo of the School of Chemical Engineering and Technology, Tianjin University, submitted at the second instance, could prove that the Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate protected by Claim 3 could be prepared. (2) Both the first-instance judgment and Decision No. 13582 erred in determining whether the disclosure was sufficient, as they failed to start from the technical problem to be solved by the present invention, leading to factual errors. Specifically: (a) Section 3.1 of Chapter 10, Part 2 of the Examination Guidelines provides that where the claimed invention is a chemical product itself, the description shall specify the identification, preparation, and use of the chemical product; for compound inventions, the description shall state the chemical name and structural formula or molecular formula of the compound... and shall record chemical and physical performance parameters related to the technical problem to be solved by the invention, so that the claimed compound can be clearly identified. Therefore, as long as the description provides chemical and physical performance parameters "related to the technical problem to be solved by the invention," it satisfies the requirement of sufficient disclosure in the chemical field. (b) The specification of the patent-in-suit clearly states that the technical problem to be solved by the present invention is: The present invention relates to a novel crystalline form of atorvastatin. Claim 3 of the patent protects Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate having the XPRD of Claim 1. A person skilled in the art should understand that the water content (3 moles of water) contained in the Type I crystalline atorvastatin protected by Claim 3 was not pre-conceived by the inventors before preparing the Type I crystal but was determined through analytical testing after obtaining the Type I crystal. In other words, whether the obtained Type I crystalline atorvastatin contains water or other solvents does not affect the outcome that the inventors obtained the technical solution, i.e., the Type I crystalline atorvastatin, for solving the technical problem. Therefore, both the first-instance judgment and Decision No. 13582 erroneously and improperly considered the water content of crystalline atorvastatin and reached the erroneous conclusion that the invention was insufficiently disclosed. (3) Regarding the identification of the Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate protected by Claim 3: (a) In Decision No. 13582, the Patent Reexamination Board imposed more stringent requirements for "identification of a compound product" than those in the Examination Guidelines. The Examination Guidelines do not require that "the structure and composition of a chemical product invention must be proven by experimental data." To achieve the purpose of the present invention, i.e., "facilitating filtration and drying in large-scale production," the inventors only needed to prepare the crystals. The Board's requirement that the description must prove by data, spectra, or preparation steps that the Type I crystalline atorvastatin obtained was a trihydrate containing 3 moles of water exceeded the requirements for compound identification under the Examination Guidelines. (b) The description of the patent-in-suit satisfies the requirements for compound product identification under the Examination Guidelines with respect to the Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate protected by Claim 3. (4) Regarding the preparation of the Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate protected by Claim 3: (a) Decision No. 13582 of the Patent Reexamination Board and the first-instance judgment failed to recognize the substantive difference between Method A of Example 1 and Example 3, leading to factual errors. (b) Decision No. 13582 imposed more stringent requirements for "preparation of a compound product" than those in the Examination Guidelines. (c) The description of the patent-in-suit satisfies the requirements for compound product preparation under the Examination Guidelines with respect to the Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate protected by Claim 3. (5) It was legally erroneous for the Patent Reexamination Board in Decision No. 13582 to require that "the description must provide evidence proving that all crystalline atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water have the same XPRD" as a condition for satisfying the sufficient disclosure requirement of Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

The Patent Reexamination Board, Jialin Company, and Zhang Chu abided by the first-instance judgment.

At the second instance, the Beijing High People's Court found the following: The facts found by the first-instance court were clear and were confirmed. During the second-instance trial, Warner-Lambert Company submitted the "Preparation and Identification Experiment Report of Atorvastatin Calcium Crystals" completed by Tianjin University (hereinafter referred to as the Tianjin University Experiment Report) to demonstrate that a person skilled in the art could implement the present invention based on the description. The experiment was completed by Associate Professor Gong Junbo on October 20, 2011, at the School of Chemical Engineering and Technology, Tianjin University. Associate Professor Gong Junbo appeared in court and was examined. During examination, Associate Professor Gong stated: By repeating Method A of Example 1 of the patent, Type I crystalline atorvastatin was prepared; a full spectrum comparison could indicate the crystal form; the experiment did not measure the water content of the Type I crystalline atorvastatin; the experiment likely contained approximately 3.3 moles of water, but further experiments were needed to determine the specific form of its existence, etc.

The second-instance court further found: Page 1 of the patent specification states: The present invention relates to novel crystalline forms of atorvastatin. Page 2 states: The methods in the above U.S. patents disclose amorphous atorvastatin, which is unsuitable for filtration and drying in large-scale production; we have now surprisingly and unexpectedly found that atorvastatin can be prepared in crystalline form; therefore, the present invention provides atorvastatin in a novel crystalline form called Type I. Type I atorvastatin consists of atorvastatin with smaller particles and a more uniform particle size distribution than the previous amorphous product, and it has more favorable properties for filtration and drying. Furthermore, Type I atorvastatin is purer and more stable than the amorphous product.

With respect to the patent-in-suit, Zhang Chu filed a request for invalidation with the Patent Reexamination Board on August 8, 2007, on the grounds that Claims 1-3 and 10-24 lacked novelty, and Claims 1-9 lacked inventiveness. The Patent Reexamination Board accepted Zhang Chu's request and consolidated it with the invalidation request filed by Jialin Company for trial.

The Beijing High People's Court held at the second instance: According to the relevant provisions of Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, Section 2.1 of Chapter 2, Part 2, Section 3.1 of Chapter 10, Part 2, Section 2.2.4 of Chapter 2, Part 2, and Section 3.2.1.1 of Chapter 4, Part 2 of the Examination Guidelines, determining whether an invention satisfies the requirement of sufficient disclosure includes identifying the technical problem to be solved by the invention. In this case, the patent specification states: The present invention relates to novel crystalline forms of atorvastatin; the published U.S. patents disclose that amorphous atorvastatin is unsuitable for filtration and drying in large-scale production; the present invention provides atorvastatin in a novel crystalline form called Type I, which consists of atorvastatin with smaller particles and a more uniform particle size distribution than the previous amorphous product, and it has more favorable properties for filtration and drying. Type I atorvastatin is purer and more stable than the amorphous product. Therefore, the technical problem to be solved by the present invention is to obtain a crystalline form of atorvastatin, specifically Type I crystalline atorvastatin, to overcome the technical problem that "amorphous atorvastatin is unsuitable for filtration and drying in large-scale production."

In Decision No. 13582, the Patent Reexamination Board considered that "water content is an indispensable part of the product composition" and concluded that the patent specification did not meet the requirement of sufficient disclosure because the specification did not provide any qualitative or quantitative data proving that the obtained Type I crystal indeed contained 1-8 moles (preferably 3 moles) of water. However, since the Patent Reexamination Board did not identify the technical problem to be solved by the present invention nor clarify which parameters were "chemical and physical performance parameters related to the technical problem to be solved," the Board's determination that the patent was insufficiently disclosed and that Claim 3 did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, without overall consideration of the technical problem to be solved by the present invention, was clearly improper. Warner-Lambert Company's related appeal grounds were well-founded and were supported.

In summary, the first-instance court's determination that Claim 3 of the patent-in-suit did not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law was erroneous, and the second-instance court corrected it. Pursuant to Article 61, Item (3) of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 70 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the second-instance court ruled as follows: 1. Revoke Administrative Judgment No. (2009) Yizhong Zhixing Chu Zi No. 2710; 2. Revoke Decision No. 13582; 3. The Patent Reexamination Board shall make a new invalidation determination regarding the patent-in-suit. The first-instance and second-instance case acceptance fees of RMB 100 each shall be borne by the Patent Reexamination Board.

Dissatisfied with the above second-instance judgment, the Patent Reexamination Board applied to this Court for retrial, arguing as follows:

(1) The second-instance judgment erred in its understanding and method of determining Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, leading to an erroneous conclusion. (a) It misunderstood the term "invention" in Article 26, Paragraph 3, resulting in an error in identifying the object of determination. First, pursuant to Article 2 of the Patent Law, the object of Article 26, Paragraph 3 should be the technical solution of the claim that serves as the published scope of rights. In analyzing whether the patent-in-suit complied with Article 26, Paragraph 3, the second-instance judgment did not analyze what the technical solution of the claim was. Second, the second-instance judgment actually took "Type I crystalline atorvastatin" as the object of the invention in this case, which is significantly different from "Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles (preferably 3 moles) of water" as defined in Claims 1-3. (b) The second-instance judgment misunderstood the meaning of "clear and complete" in Article 26, Paragraph 3. The text of Claims 1-3 clearly indicates that the subject matter protected is Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing a specific amount of water, and the confirmation of water content is one of the essential technical contents for clearly understanding and implementing the present invention. A person skilled in the art cannot directly derive from the prior art that products within the water content range defined in Claims 1-3 will all have the XPRD data as defined; the patentee has the obligation to clearly and completely explain this in the description. Furthermore, the primary condition for sufficient disclosure of a compound is that a person skilled in the art can, based on the disclosure of the description, identify its structure and confirm the existence of the structured product. This is a direct requirement of Article 26, Paragraph 3 for compound inventions. However, the patent-in-suit merely states in the description that "Type I crystalline atorvastatin contains about 1 to 8 moles of water, preferably, Type I atorvastatin contains 3 moles of water," without measuring and recording the water content of the obtained product in the examples. Therefore, a person skilled in the art cannot confirm that the patentee had indeed obtained the product with the specific water content claimed before the filing date. (c) The second-instance judgment misunderstood the meaning of "solving its technical problem" in the Examination Guidelines, leading to errors in the reasoning and methodology. There is a strict internal logic among implementing the technical solution of the invention or utility model, solving its technical problem, and producing the expected technical effect. First, discussing whether a technical solution can solve its technical problem necessarily presupposes determining what the technical solution is. Second, whether an invention solves its technical problem is certainly related to the objective effect achieved by the technical means adopted in the invention's technical solution, but the implicit prerequisite for solving the technical problem claimed by the invention through the technical solution is that the technical solution has indeed been obtained and can be realized. It can be said that the identification and preparation of the chemical product are the minimum requirements for "solving its technical problem." In the absence of sufficient disclosure at the level of preparation and identification, Decision No. 13582 did not need to further discuss whether the technical problem at the effect level was solved. In summary, the second-instance judgment erred in its understanding of Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, as well as in the object, logical sequence, and methodology of determination, leading to an erroneous conclusion.

(2) Regarding the status of water content measurement data: (a) Water content is not a performance parameter directly characterizing the nature and function of the products in Claims 1-3; as a product element in a hydrate, it is a structural and compositional feature of the product. Therefore, water content measurement data, as evidence proving the actual existence state of the product, is an indispensable part of product identification. (b) Claims 1-3 define crystalline hydrates that show the same XPRD at different water contents; the description asserts that for atorvastatin, the hydrated form and the non-hydrated form are equivalent, i.e., the presence of water does not affect the XPRD of the crystal. However, in the art, there is no uniform teaching as to whether water in a specific compound's hydrate is lattice water that enters the crystal lattice or channel water that does not. Therefore, for a specific compound like atorvastatin and a specific crystal form like Type I, without prior art for reference and without any logical theoretical analysis in the description, a person skilled in the art cannot determine which type of hydrate it is, i.e., they cannot confirm whether the technical solutions of Claims 1-3 actually exist and can be realized. Since the patentee asserted in the description that the hydrated and non-hydrated forms are equivalent and claimed a technical solution where the water content can vary within a specific range of 1-8 moles but the XPRD data remains unchanged, the patentee should bear the corresponding burden of proof for this assertion and the adverse consequences of failure to meet that burden. (c) Confirming whether the bound water in the products of Claims 1-3 is lattice water or channel water, and the specific water content, is also crucial for analyzing and determining whether the technical problem at the effect level can be solved. A person skilled in the art knows that for a specific form of an active ingredient intended for pharmaceutical use, if the form itself does not meet the quantitative and stability requirements for final drug manufacturing and is difficult to use in pharmaceutical preparations, then discussing whether the form facilitates filtration and drying during preparation is meaningless. Specifically for this patent, for the form of water in the crystalline hydrate, lattice water that enters the crystal lattice should be relatively stable due to the stability of the lattice itself. However, channel hydrates have lower tolerance to potentially changing environmental conditions during preparation, thus affecting the accurate quantification of the active ingredient during pharmaceutical preparation. Therefore, where the description of the patent-in-suit does not prove the type to which the products of Claims 1-3 belong and does not clearly and completely explain whether they can ultimately be used to prepare pharmaceutical preparations, a person skilled in the art cannot determine whether the products of Claims 1-3 can achieve the fundamental purpose of being used to prepare pharmaceutical preparations.

(3) Regarding the social impact of this case. The patent-in-suit has patent family members in Europe, Japan, and the United States, and these family patents have been in constant dispute after grant. Among them, the European and Japanese family patents have been revoked or invalidated. Furthermore, the conclusion of this case involves significant national economic interests and public health, and has strong guiding significance for the current understanding and application of the examination standard for Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law in the pharmaceutical field, with a huge ripple effect from the case.

In summary, the Patent Reexamination Board requested this Court to retry the case according to law, revoke the second-instance judgment, and uphold Decision No. 13582.

Jialin Company, dissatisfied with the above second-instance judgment, applied to this Court for retrial, arguing as follows:

(1) The second-instance judgment erred in both fact-finding and application of law. (a) Before determining whether an invention can solve the technical problem, it is necessary to consider whether the description clearly and completely explains what the invention is and whether it is technically feasible. The focus of dispute among the parties in this case was the identification and availability of the product defined by the claims of the patent-in-suit. The second-instance judgment did not express any opinion on this issue at all, but instead directly required the Patent Reexamination Board to analyze which "chemical and physical performance parameters" are related to solving the technical problem of "filtration and drying," and then, from the multiple essential technical features defined in the claims, only select those chemical and physical performance parameters that meet the needs of "filtration and drying" to determine whether these required parameters are clearly and completely described. This approach was clearly improper. (b) The second-instance judgment erred in its determination of the "invention." The water in the product defined by Claim 1 of the patent-in-suit is an essential component, while the X-ray powder diffraction data characteristics characterize the crystal structure of the product from another angle; both are essential technical features of the claim and need to be clearly and completely described in the specification. (c) The second-instance judgment erroneously determined the "technical problem to be solved." For the product invention defined by Claims 1-3 of the patent-in-suit, combined with the content of the specification, meeting strict pharmaceutical requirements and specification formulations, and having better manufacturing and storage stability are the primary and essential technical problems to be solved, not merely obtaining the general commonality of crystals relative to amorphous forms—facilitation of filtration and drying. (d) For a crystal form invention, the technical problem it must necessarily solve is the stability of water content and storage stability of the invented product, so as to facilitate accurate dispensing and meet the strict requirements of pharmaceutical preparations for specification formulations. Therefore, water content and its form are not only literally technical features of the technical solutions of Claims 1-3 of the patent-in-suit but are also indispensable essential technical features directly and necessarily related to the technical problem to be solved by the technical solution. Consequently, from the perspective of the technical problem to be solved by the invention, in determining what the invention is and the technical problem to be solved, water content and its form characteristics should not be ignored.

(2) The patent specification is insufficiently disclosed, failing to meet the requirements of Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law. 1. The patent specification does not disclose measurement data or spectra that can be used to confirm the water content and stable form of the product. Water content and stable form are essential technical features that are directly related to the technical problem to be solved by the invention in the Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate defined in claims 1-3, and are elements of the composition and crystal structure of the product. Therefore, providing measurement data for water content and stable form is an indispensable part of product confirmation and is a basic disclosure obligation that the patentee should fulfill commensurate with the scope of protection claimed in claims 1-3. A person skilled in the art, based on the content disclosed in the patent specification, cannot clearly confirm that the patentee actually obtained the crystalline product having a specific water content and form as protected in claims 1-3, let alone further determine whether the water described therein would affect the solution of the technical problem, and to what extent. Moreover, where the prior art provides no teaching and the specification provides no logical theoretical analysis, a person skilled in the art simply cannot confirm whether the same set of diffraction features recorded in claims 1-3 truly represents the diffraction features of Type I crystalline atorvastatin having different water contents. 2. A person skilled in the art, based on the content disclosed in the specification, cannot prepare the product protected in claims 1-3. First, a person skilled in the art cannot implement the content of Example 1 of the patent specification. In Example 1, whether Method A or Method B, Type I crystalline atorvastatin seed crystals are used, but the patent specification does not provide an implementation method for obtaining the seed crystals, nor does it state the source of the seed crystals. Therefore, in the absence of being able to obtain the seed crystals, a person skilled in the art cannot reproduce the operational scheme of Example 1. Second, based on the general description in the patent specification, a person skilled in the art cannot confirm that the product defined in claims 1-3 will necessarily be obtained without adding seed crystals.

In summary, Jialin Company requests this Court to retry this case according to law, and to render a judgment setting aside the second-instance judgment and upholding Decision No. 13582.

Warner-Lambert Company submitted its opinion stating: (1) Regarding the relationship between the technical problem to be solved by the present invention and the sufficiency of disclosure in the specification. To determine whether a compound patent meets the requirement of sufficient disclosure under Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, identifying the technical problem to be solved by the invention is the foundation and key. First, one must start from the prior art to understand what technical problem the invention aims to solve, and then determine, with respect to that technical problem, which information is essential and should be fully disclosed in the specification, and which information is irrelevant to the technical problem to be solved and therefore need not be described in detail in the specification. The technical problem to be solved by the present invention is "to obtain Type I crystalline atorvastatin" to overcome the disadvantage that "amorphous atorvastatin is unsuitable for filtration and drying in large-scale production". In Decision No. 13582, the Patent Reexamination Board failed to consider this foundational and key issue of "the technical problem solved by the present invention", and also failed to consider which parameters are "chemical and physical performance parameters related to the technical problem to be solved", erroneously considered and discussed the water content of Type I crystalline atorvastatin, and ultimately reached the erroneous conclusion that the present invention is insufficiently disclosed. The second-instance judgment corrected the above errors of the Reexamination Board, found the facts clearly, and applied the law correctly, and should be upheld. (2) The disclosure of the technical solutions of claims 1-3 in the patent specification meets the requirement of "capable of being realized" under the Patent Law and the Guidelines for Examination. A person skilled in the art, guided by the teaching of the patent specification and combined with general knowledge and skills in the field, can easily select specific reaction conditions from the range of reaction conditions disclosed in the examples of the specification, and can obtain Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water (preferably 3 moles of water) with at most a few attempts and reasonable adjustments to these conditions. (3) Regarding the confirmation of the water content in Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate. First, the disclosure of the patent specification meets the two-level requirements for compound confirmation under the Guidelines for Examination. The Patent Reexamination Board's requirement that the patent specification must use experimental data to prove the water content of the crystal, and must strictly prove from the original experimental data, spectra, or based on the preparation steps that the Type I crystalline atorvastatin obtained by the inventor contains 1-8 moles of water, preferably 3 moles of water, exceeds the requirements of the Guidelines for Examination and is without basis. Second, although the examples in the patent specification do not record the water content of the obtained Type I crystalline atorvastatin, a person skilled in the art, after reading the entire content of the patent claims and specification, can understand and believe that the patentee had prepared Type I crystalline atorvastatin trihydrate before the priority date. With respect to the explicit statement in the fourth paragraph from the bottom on page 15 of the specification: "Type I atorvastatin contains about 1-8 moles of water. Preferably, Type I atorvastatin contains 3 moles of water", a person skilled in the art would understand that the water content was not preconceived before obtaining the crystalline form of atorvastatin, but must have been measured after preparing the Type I crystal. That is, the inventor performed a water content measurement on the obtained Type I crystalline atorvastatin, and the water content recorded here is a result summarized from the experimental data. (4) The term "water" in the "Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate" defined in the claims should be understood in a broad sense as water of crystallization, which may include lattice water and channel water. Before the priority date of this patent, persons skilled in the art were well aware that channel hydrates have the property of retaining the same crystal structure while gaining or losing a certain amount of water. Since the patent specification has already clearly recorded the characteristics of Type I crystalline atorvastatin: namely, it has characteristic XPRD peaks that distinguish it from amorphous atorvastatin and other atorvastatin crystalline forms in this patent, and contains about 1 to 8 moles of water, preferably 3 moles of water, a person skilled in the art can thereby appreciate that this new crystal designated as "Type I crystal" in this patent should be a channel hydrate, i.e., its water content can vary within a certain range without causing changes in the characteristic XPRD peaks of the crystal. Furthermore, whether Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrates containing 1-8 moles of water all have the same XPRD is not a matter of sufficiency of disclosure in the specification, but a matter of whether the claims are supported by the specification. (5) Regarding the social impact of this case. Although this case involves a pharmaceutical product with global leading sales, the sales volume of the product is unrelated to whether the patent specification meets the requirement of sufficient disclosure. The Patent Reexamination Board's emphasis on this reason in the retrial procedure lacks legal basis. In summary, Warner-Lambert Company believes that the second-instance judgment found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly, and requests this Court to dismiss the retrial applications of the two retrial applicants according to law.

Third Party Zhang Chu stated its opinion: It agrees with the opinions of the two retrial applicants in this case.

During the second-instance proceedings, Warner-Lambert Company submitted an experimental report from Tianjin University, which involved two experiments: 1. Preparation of atorvastatin calcium Type I crystalline trihydrate according to Method A of Example 1 of this patent; 2. Preparation of atorvastatin calcium Type I crystalline trihydrate without using seed crystals according to the records on lines 6 to 14 of page 16 of the patent specification. The conclusions of both experiments confirmed that atorvastatin calcium Type I crystalline trihydrate was prepared. During the retrial hearing, Jialin Company argued that Warner-Lambert Company only submitted this evidence when the second-instance hearing was opened, and without any preparation, it was unable to fully cross-examine Associate Professor Gong Junbo, the person who completed the report. To further ascertain the facts, with the consent of the parties, this Court arranged for Jialin Company to submit written cross-examination questions to Associate Professor Gong Junbo, who responded in writing. The main opinions of the Patent Reexamination Board and Jialin Company regarding the evidence were: 1. The completing unit, the School of Chemical Engineering and Technology of Tianjin University, and the person who completed it, Associate Professor Gong Junbo, do not have the qualifications of a technical and legal expert for identification. 2. This evidence constitutes new evidence that should not be considered in administrative litigation proceedings. 3. Experiment 1 of this evidence adopted a scheme of adding seed crystals, but this patent does not disclose the source of the seed crystals or the method for obtaining them. The selection of operating conditions for the critical crystallization step in the experiment of this evidence far exceeds the teaching given to persons skilled in the art by the patent specification. In Method A of Example 1 of the patent in suit, after adding the seed crystals, it is recorded as "heating the mixture at 51-57°C for at least 10 minutes, then cooling to 15-40°C." In Experiment 1 of the Tianjin University experimental report, the corresponding heating time was "17 hours," which is not on the same order of magnitude as "at least 10 minutes." Furthermore, this patent does not state that cooling from 51-57°C to 15-40°C requires special control. According to the general understanding of a person skilled in the art, it should be static cooling or natural cooling. However, in Experiment 1 of the Tianjin University experimental report, cooling from about 53°C to room temperature took as long as 10 hours, which is obviously a special cooling method using special control measures, and the time was greatly extended. In Experiment 2 of the Tianjin University experimental report, the mixture was "stirred overnight" (generally understood as 12-17 hours) at 52-57°C, and the slurry was cooled from 52-57°C to room temperature over 10 hours. As noted above, this is also far from the "at least 10 minutes" and "cooling" recorded in Method A of Example 1 of the patent specification. 4. Experiment 2 of this evidence cannot prove that it obtained Type I crystalline atorvastatin calcium trihydrate as defined in claim 3 of this patent.

During this Court's review of the retrial application, Jialin Company submitted the "Expert Opinion on Judicial Appraisal" (Beijing Guowei [2013] Zhi Si Jian Zi No. 11, hereinafter the "Expert Opinion") issued by the Beijing Guowei Judicial Appraisal Center for Intellectual Property, to prove that the patent is insufficiently disclosed, that the reaction crystallization experimental scheme disclosed in the patent specification cannot yield Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water, and that the scheme of Experiment 2 in the Tianjin University experimental report submitted by Warner-Lambert Company in the second instance exceeded the scope disclosed in the patent specification, and the product of Experiment 2 differed from the Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as described in the patent. During the hearing of the retrial application review in this Court, the appraisal experts and testing personnel appeared in court to present their opinions and underwent cross-examination by all parties. Warner-Lambert Company's main opinions on this Expert Opinion were: 1. The Expert Opinion does not meet the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Law and relevant judicial interpretations for submitting evidence and should not be considered. 2. The subject matter of appraisal in the Expert Opinion was not involved in Decision No. 13582, has no relevance to this case, and should not be considered. 3. The design of the experimental scheme for appraisal in the Expert Opinion violates the common knowledge of persons skilled in the art and should not be adopted. (a) The design of the reaction crystallization experimental scheme in the appraisal subject matter violates common knowledge in the field. Regarding the reaction crystallization time, the Expert Opinion simply relied on the "heating for at least 10 minutes" from Method A of Example 1 of the patent specification and concluded that "according to common knowledge, it can be determined that the heating time is more than 10 minutes, generally not exceeding 1 hour, therefore the heating time is set at 15 minutes to 60 minutes". Regarding the cooling method, the Expert Opinion stated: "natural cooling is used to cool the mixture" because "the specification does not specifically mention cooling, so a person skilled in the art defaults to natural cooling". However, the appraiser did not adopt the perspective of a person skilled in the art and overlooked the important difference that Method A of Example 1 of the patent specification is a large-scale industrial method with a total reaction volume exceeding 1,300 liters, while the appraiser conducted a small-scale experiment with a total reaction volume of about 125 milliliters, scaled down by a factor of 10,000 from the above industrial scale. Due to the difference in scale, even if both experiments used "natural cooling" to lower the temperature, a person skilled in the art would know that their cooling rates would be vastly different. For methods of preparing compound crystals from solution, the cooling rate is an important factor in the successful preparation of compound crystals. Furthermore, according to the general teaching of the reaction crystallization method in the second paragraph, line 7 of page 16 of the patent specification, a person skilled in the art would know that the crystallization step in the reaction crystallization method is preferably carried out at elevated temperatures, such as about 45-60°C, preferably 47-52°C. According to the experimental scheme designed by the appraiser, the reactants were maintained at a high temperature above 40°C for less than 1 hour, which is clearly insufficient time for crystal nucleation and growth. Based on common knowledge, persons skilled in the art all know that to prepare crystals from solution, the solution system must be slowly cooled and left for a long time. It is evident that the experimental scheme designed by the appraiser did not simulate the temperature profile of Method A of Example 1 of the patent. The cooling rate of the reactant system was too fast, and the crystal formation process was too short. Such an operation method does not respect the objective laws of crystal formation, and therefore it is natural that Type I crystalline atorvastatin was not obtained. (b) The Expert Opinion concluded that the experimental product of Experiment 2 of the Tianjin University experimental report is different from the Type I crystalline atorvastatin hydrate containing 1-8 moles of water as defined in claim 1 of this patent. This conclusion should not be adopted. The Patent Reexamination Board and Zhang Chu expressed no objection to the Expert Opinion.

Evidence 20 already indicates that the diffraction peak intensities in X-ray powder diffraction patterns can be measured semi-quantitatively, with a maximum allowable variation of 20%.
